hallmark: the shield outline, with a scutellum a third of its length and pale wing tips crossed over the abdomen

reference.title: Pentatoma prasina, from The Hemiptera Heteroptera of the British Islands, plate 3, fig. 1

doc: *Palomena prasina*, dorsal — the green shield bug.
Traced from figure 1 of Robert Morgan's plate 3 for Edward Saunders's *The
Hemiptera Heteroptera of the British Islands* (1892), where it is captioned
under its old name *Pentatoma prasina*;
`references/palomena-prasina.jpg` is the plate and `references/SOURCES.md`
has the provenance.
## The first true bug in the collection
Which is why the outline matters more here than the pattern. A shield bug is
recognised as a shape before it is recognised as a species: a broad pentagon
with the widest point behind the middle, a pronotum whose lateral angles are
rounded rather than spined, and a scutellum — the triangle between the folded
wings — running a third of the way down the back. `REQUIRED_PARTS.hemiptera`
asks for that scutellum for exactly this reason.
## Half a wing is a window and half is not
A hemelytron is hard at the base and membranous at the tip, which is what the
suborder is named for. The membranes cross over each other on the midline and
reach past the end of the abdomen, and in the lithograph they are the one pale
thing on a green animal. They are drawn as a `surface` fill — bare paper —
rather than with `opacity: 'membrane'`: what is behind them here is the other
wing and the tip of the abdomen, and the reference does not show either
through. The dragonfly is the plate that needs a real window.
## No hindwings
They are folded underneath and nothing of them shows from above, so none are
drawn and `REQUIRED_PARTS.hemiptera` does not ask for them.
## Plate space
y = 0 at the front of the head, y = 1000 at the tip of the abdomen — which for
this animal is the tip of the folded wing membranes, because they overhang it.
The antennae reach to about y = -250 and the legs out to x = 455, both well
outside the body's own box, which is what `plateViewBox` measures for.

note: Legs first, so they pass under the body.
Femora and tibiae are capsules measured across at about six and four per
cent of the width across the wings, which is the proportion CLAUDE.md
records and the reference bears out: a shield bug's legs are slender and
the animal reads as moulded rather than engraved when they are not.
The abdomen, which shows only as a rim.
Almost all of it is under the wings; what a reader sees is the connexivum,
the strip of abdominal margin standing out beyond them. Drawn whole
anyway, because the wings are placed against it and a rim authored as a
rim would have to be re-measured the first time a wing moved.
The connexivum, as five ticks rather than five bands.
The lithograph alternates pale and dark along the abdominal margin. At
eighty pixels that is a dotted line and at six hundred it is five
segments; either way it is the segment boundaries that carry it, so the
boundaries are what is drawn.
One hemelytron: hardened at the base, membranous at the tip.
The inner edge runs down the side of the scutellum, then along the midline
where the two wings cross over each other. A landmark on the midline gets
a vertical tangent from the builder, so the seam between a wing and its
own reflection is a line rather than a pinch.
The claval suture — the fold between the two hard parts of the wing.
One line, because at plate size it is one line.
The punctation, as hatching.
The corium is densely pitted and the lithograph stipples it. Stipple is
not in this project's vocabulary — three line weights are — so it becomes
a fan of strokes running the length of the wing, which is what the
engraving convention does with a pitted surface.
The membrane: bare paper, not a window.
`opacity: 'membrane'` would be the wrong tool. What is behind this wing
tip is the other wing tip and the end of the abdomen, and the reference
shows neither through it — it is opaque and pale. The dragonfly is the
plate where a wing has to be transparent.
The scutellum, which is the order seen from above.
A third of the length of the animal, with slightly hollowed sides and a
blunt tip. Drawn once, on the axis: it straddles the midline and is
symmetric in itself, so reflecting it would put a second copy a hair off
the first and show as a doubled line down the middle of the back.
The pronotum: broad, and rounded at the shoulders.
The lateral angles are the character. *Palomena* has them rounded; the
genera a key separates it from have them drawn out into points, and a
plate that squares them off has drawn a different animal.
The head, drawn once on the axis for the same reason as the scutellum.
The two lobes in front of the eyes meet ahead of the clypeus, which is
the blunt front margin the outline ends in.
Five segments, drawn as three strokes and a tip.
The joints are what a reader sees at plate size, not the count. The last
two segments are darker and thicker than the first three in the
lithograph, so the tip is a filled capsule rather than the end of a
tapering line.
